transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Thank you. Well, what finally scared me into making this appointment is... I've been having these thoughts lately. Like, I'll just be sitting there and I think, "If I didn't wake up tomorrow, that might be easier." I definitely don't want to hurt myself! I really don't. It just... it spooked me to catch myself thinking that way. 

Which is funny because usually nothing spooks me. I'm a supervisor in retail, and let me tell you, you see absolutely everything there. Just last week we had a woman try to return a blender she clearly bought in, like, 2015. She didn't even have a receipt, and she yelled at my newest cashier for twenty minutes. I had to step in, and honestly, I have a bachelor's degree, I really shouldn't be arguing with people about ten-year-old kitchen appliances at my age, but that's retail for you. The general public is just wild sometimes. They really don't read the store policies. 

But anyway, yes... those thoughts about just not waking up. I figured I should probably come in and talk to someone about that.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not waking up?

Gosh, I'm not really sure exactly when it started. Time just sort of blurs together lately, you know? It’s a lot like how our store schedules work... we make them three weeks in advance, but then corporate changes the promotional calendar at the absolute last minute. Just yesterday, my district manager called—right in the middle of my lunch break, which is supposed to be my protected time—to tell me we have to completely reset the front end of the store for the spring rollout. In February! I mean, who is buying outdoor patio cushions in February? But that's corporate for you, sitting in their climate-controlled offices not realizing it's still snowing here. It drives my team crazy, and I'm the one who has to smooth it all over and pretend it makes sense. It’s exhausting just thinking about it, honestly. 

But... I'm sorry, what was the question again? Oh, the thoughts about not waking up. Right. Yeah, I really couldn't give you a specific timeline. I just haven't really kept track.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time lately?

Well, yeah, I suppose so. Most mornings lately, I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling... it's just like the color has completely drained out of everything before I even get dressed for the store. 

And speaking of getting dressed, you would not believe the new dress code corporate just rolled out for us. They want all the supervisors wearing these stiff, navy blue vests. Navy blue! Do you know how impossible it is to keep navy blue looking clean when you're dealing with retail freight? Between the dust from the cardboard boxes in the stockroom and just general store lint, it's a total nightmare. I have to buy those sticky lint rollers in bulk now just to look professional. My husband, bless his heart, he tries to help out by doing the laundry on my long shifts, but he always washes my work clothes with the bath towels. You absolutely cannot wash a navy poly-blend with white cotton towels! I've explained it to him a hundred times, but he just doesn't look at the tags. It completely ruins the fabric and I spend twenty minutes picking fuzz off myself. It's just one more thing to manage, you know? 

But... um, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah. Before I even put that awful vest on, I just feel... gray. Just empty and heavy.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like, or has that changed lately?

Well, it's definitely changed. Like with my art. I still set out my paints at home, or I'll think about going to my pottery class... but honestly, the studio I go to for pottery is right downtown, and the parking situation there is just atrocious right now. They've been doing construction on Main Street for what feels like six months. They dig up the pipes, fill the hole, and then two weeks later, they dig it right back up again! It makes absolutely no sense. My husband says it's a municipal budget thing, but I think it's just poor city planning. 

It backs up traffic all the way to the interstate, which is exactly the route half my cashiers take to get to the store. No wonder everyone is always five minutes late clocking in these days. I keep telling the district manager we need to temporarily adjust the attendance grace period because of the roadwork, but she just quotes the corporate handbook at me over email. It's like talking to a brick wall. They really have no idea what it's like on the ground level.

Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, my hobbies. Right. Well, even if I don't go to the class and I just stay home and set up my easel, it's the same thing. I'll get all the materials out, but when I sit down, I just stare at them. I feel absolutely none of the spark I used to feel. It's just... nothing.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

Well, I mean, I guess I just said it, didn't I? I still try. I really do. I'll get my paints out, or I'll think about that pottery class... but speaking of the pottery class, the instructor there, Susan, she just retired. And the new girl they brought in to replace her—she's practically a child! I swear she can't be a day over twenty-two. She plays this awful, loud electronic music during the studio time. How is anyone supposed to center clay on a wheel with that thump-thump-thump going on in the background? It's exactly like what corporate did with the store radio last month. They switched our station from the easy listening mix to some top-40 pop channel because they said it would "energize the customer experience." Energize! All it does is give my closing shift a migraine. I had two cashiers threaten to walk out last week because they had to listen to the same pop song four times in an eight-hour shift. I had to go into the manager's office and physically unplug the speaker wire just to get some peace. 

But... oh, goodness, I'm rambling again. I'm sorry. You were asking if there's anything I still enjoy. Um... no. Like I was saying, even when I sit down with my paints, I just stare at them. There's just no spark anymore. None at all.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

Anxious? No, not really. I mean, I don't feel on edge or anything like that. Though, speaking of being on edge, my sister called me yesterday in an absolute panic about her retirement account. She's been watching the news non-stop, and you know how they make every little dip in the market sound like the end of the world. I told her, 'Linda, you're not touching that money for another five years, just turn off the television.' But she won't listen. She's always been high-strung, ever since we were kids. I remember when we were in high school, she would get so worked up before exams that she'd make herself sick. 

And now she's got it in her head that she needs to move all her investments into gold. Gold! Can you imagine? I tried to explain to her that her financial advisor probably knows better than some talking head on a cable news channel, but she just talks right over me. It's exactly like dealing with the regional manager when he comes in for a store walk. He comes in, completely ignores the actual sales data I've prepared for him, and starts pointing out dust on the baseboards or asking why a display isn't angled exactly forty-five degrees. It's maddening. 

But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right. Feeling anxious. No, I wouldn't say I feel anxious. Just heavy and tired, mostly.
Are there any small, everyday things that you still look forward to?

Well, I suppose I try to look forward to things. Like I mentioned, I'll still get my paints out, or I'll try to plan to go to my pottery class. But honestly, speaking of everyday things, my neighbor's dog has been barking incessantly every single morning at 6:00 AM. It's a little terrier mix, and I swear it has the most piercing bark I've ever heard. The neighbor, Tom, he just lets it out in the yard and goes back to sleep. I tried to talk to him about it over the fence last week, but he just shrugged and said, 'Dogs will be dogs.' It's so inconsiderate! It reminds me of this one customer we get at the store—she comes in every Tuesday, lets her toddler run wild pulling things off the bottom shelves, and just smiles while my cashiers have to follow behind them picking up merchandise. People just have no sense of personal responsibility anymore. It's like everyone expects someone else to clean up their mess, whether it's literal or figurative. 

Oh, gosh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm so sorry. I keep getting sidetracked. You asked about looking forward to things. But yeah, like I said before... even when I try to do the small things I used to like, like setting out my art materials, I just end up staring at them. There's just no spark. I don't feel anything from it anymore.
Are there any activities, no matter how small, that you still find give you some pleasure?

Well, I think... I mean, we just talked about this, didn't we? I try. I really do try to find something. I'll still set out my paints on the kitchen table, or I'll think about going down to the studio for pottery class. But honestly, speaking of the kitchen table, I noticed this morning that one of the legs is getting wobbly again. I bought that table at an estate sale fifteen years ago, back when my husband and I lived in the old house on Elm Street. It was a beautiful house, had this wrap-around porch that was just lovely in the spring. But the maintenance! Oh, it was a nightmare. The gutters were always clogging with oak leaves, and the basement smelled like damp earth no matter how many dehumidifiers we ran. It's just like the stockroom at work—no matter how many times I put in a work order for the HVAC, it's always freezing in the winter and sweltering in the summer. Corporate says it's an "older building quirk," but I say it's just them being cheap. 

But anyway... what were we saying? Oh, right, pleasure. Yeah, like I said before... I'll set out the paints, or I'll get to the pottery studio, and I just... I just stare at the materials. I sit there and look at them, and I feel absolutely none of the spark I used to feel. It's just gone.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Weight? No, I don't think so. My clothes still fit the same as they always do. Though, speaking of clothes, I had to completely reorganize the winter apparel section at the store yesterday because someone—and I'm pretty sure it was the new girl, Sarah—decided to mix the heavy wool coats with the lightweight windbreakers. It was a complete disaster. I spent three hours just sorting by material and color. It's like people don't understand basic visual merchandising anymore. I remember when I first started in retail, my manager, Mr. Henderson, would have had a fit if he saw a display looking that sloppy. He was a real stickler for the rules. He used to make us use a measuring tape to ensure the space between hangers was exactly one and a half inches. Can you believe that? A measuring tape! 

But, you know, it taught me discipline. Which is more than I can say for my nephew. He just dropped out of college for the second time to 'find himself.' My sister is beside herself, but I told her, 'Linda, you've been coddling him since he was a toddler, what did you expect?' 

Oh, dear. I'm rambling again, aren't I? I'm sorry. What was the question? Weight loss? Right. No, I haven't noticed any weight loss. Everything seems pretty much the same in that department.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, gray feeling in the mornings?

Well, let me think... that heavy, gray feeling. It's been a while. I'd say this low, flat part has been hanging around for about six months now. It's been long enough that my usual routines, you know, my art classes and my morning walks, they just stopped feeling restorative at all. 

Speaking of morning walks, I used to walk down by the lake every day at 7:00 AM sharp. There's this one path that goes right past Mrs. Gable's garden. She has the most incredible hydrangeas, just massive blooms, all these deep blues and purples. She told me once her secret is adding coffee grounds to the soil. I tried that with my own garden, but all I got was a bunch of ants. Millions of them! They marched right up the porch steps and into the kitchen. I had to call the exterminator, and he charged me an arm and a leg. Said it was a "specialized treatment." I swear, any time you need a professional to look at something around the house, they just see dollar signs. It's like when the transmission went out on my old Honda. The mechanic told me it would be cheaper to just buy a new car. A new car! In this economy? 

I'm sorry, I did it again. I completely lost my train of thought. You asked how long it's been. Yes, about six months of this... this grayness.
Are there any things that you used to enjoy doing, but no longer find pleasure in?

Well, yes... I mean, I think I mentioned this earlier, actually. It's the art stuff. I still try, you know? I'll set out my paints on the kitchen table, or I'll get myself all the way down to the studio for pottery class. But when I'm actually there... I just sit and stare at the materials. There's just none of that spark I used to feel. 

And speaking of the pottery studio, they just raised their monthly membership fee again. It's absolutely ridiculous. They claim it's because the cost of clay and glaze has gone up, but I happen to know the owner, Barbara, just bought a second home down in Florida. Boca Raton, I think it was. Or maybe Naples? I can't remember, but my sister Linda went to Naples for her honeymoon back in '85. It rained the entire week. They ended up spending most of their time in the hotel lounge playing gin rummy. Linda said it was a disaster, but honestly, her husband—my ex-brother-in-law, Gary—was always such a bore anyway. He used to chew his food so loudly you could hear it over the television. We'd be trying to watch Jeopardy, and all you could hear was Gary crunching on ice cubes. 

I don't know how Linda put up with it for ten years. I really don't. But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the things I used to enjoy. Yes, the painting and the pottery... I try to do them, but it's just... I just stare at everything now. The feeling is just gone.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to find enjoyable?

Well, like I was just saying... I think you just asked me that, didn't you? About the things I used to enjoy? But yes, it's exactly like that. I've completely lost interest. I mean, I still go through the motions. I'll set out my watercolors on the kitchen island, or I'll tell myself I'm going to head down to the pottery studio. But then I get there, and I just sit and stare at the clay or the blank paper. The spark is just... it's just completely gone. 

Which is a shame, really, because I just bought this beautiful set of sable brushes. They weren't cheap, either. I had to order them from a specialty shop in New York. You can't find good quality art supplies around here anymore since that little shop on Main Street closed down. The owner, Mr. Abernathy, he retired and moved to Arizona. Sedona, I think. People say Sedona is very spiritual, with all those red rocks and vortexes. I read an article in a magazine at the dentist's office last week about how people go there to align their chakras. I don't know if I believe in all that, but the dentist—Dr. Evans—he certainly believes in charging a premium for a simple cleaning. He has this new hygienist who practically interrogates you about your flossing habits. It's like, 'Listen, honey, I'm 62 years old, I think I know how to use dental floss.' 

But anyway... yes. The painting, the pottery... the interest is just gone. I just stare at it all.
Do you think you'll ever regain interest in your art and hobbies, or does it feel like that part of you is gone for good?

I honestly do not know if it is gone for good. I really hope not. Like I feel like I keep saying, I do still try to force it. I will literally set out my paints on the table, or I will get all dressed and think about driving to pottery class, but then I just end up staring at the materials. That spark I used to have is just completely missing. 

It makes me think about this one painting I did years ago of a lighthouse when I still had that spark. We went to Maine for a long weekend. Kennebunkport. Beautiful place, but the seafood gave my husband terrible food poisoning. We were supposed to go on a whale watching tour, but he was stuck in the bathroom of the bed and breakfast for two days straight. The wallpaper in that bathroom was atrocious, too. Tiny little sailboats on a mustard yellow background. Who chooses mustard yellow for a bathroom? 

It is exactly like the people who design the floor layouts at the retail store I supervise. I manage the home goods section, and corporate always sends down these diagrams that make absolutely no sense. Last week they wanted us to put the decorative throw pillows right next to the kitchen appliances. Pillows and toasters! I told the regional manager that nobody buying a blender is looking for a velvet throw pillow. He just gave me this blank look. He is nice enough, but he wears these awful clip-on ties and... wait, I am rambling again, aren't I? 

You were asking if the art is gone for good. I just do not know. I just know right now, I sit there with my supplies and feel absolutely nothing.
Have you been feeling this way for more than two years?

Two years? Oh, no, no, not that long. This current... this low, flat feeling where I just sit and stare at my paints, it's been going on for about six months now. It's been long enough that I've completely stopped doing my morning walks, too, and my art classes just don't feel restorative at all anymore. 

Which is a shame about the walks, really, because the neighborhood is usually so lovely in the mornings. Well, except for the Henderson's dog. They have this terrier mix that barks at absolutely everything. A leaf blows across the street, and that dog acts like it's a home invasion. I've tried talking to Sarah Henderson about it, but she just says, 'Oh, Buster is just protecting his territory.' Protecting it from what, Sarah? The wind? 

She's always been a bit defensive, though. We used to be on the HOA board together back in 2018, and she threw an absolute fit when we voted to change the approved exterior paint colors. She wanted to paint her shutters this awful shade of teal. Teal! In a neighborhood of colonial-style homes. It would have looked like a Miami Vice set. I remember my husband—this was before he passed, of course—he said if she painted those shutters teal, he was going to plant a row of giant arborvitae right along the property line just so he wouldn't have to look at it. He always loved his landscaping, my husband. Spent every Saturday out there with his pruning shears. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, the timeline. Right. No, it hasn't been two years. Just about six months of this... this flatness.
Have you experienced periods of feeling this low and uninterested in things before, or is this the first time?

Well, I... I'm not really sure if I've felt exactly like this before. I mean, I've had times where I was tired, certainly. Working retail will do that to you. Especially during the holidays. Oh, the holidays are just a nightmare. Last Christmas, we had this promotion on scented candles, and I swear the smell of artificial pine and cinnamon gave me a migraine that lasted from Thanksgiving until New Year's. And the music! If I have to hear Mariah Carey one more time, I might just walk out the door and never come back. 

We used to have such lovely Christmases when the kids were little. My daughter, Emily, she was always so obsessed with the Nutcracker. We took her to see the ballet in the city when she was seven, and she insisted on wearing this itchy tulle skirt the entire train ride. The conductor was this sweet older gentleman who gave her a little paper ticket to punch herself. You just don't see customer service like that anymore. Now, you get on the train and everyone is just staring at their phones, completely disconnected from the world around them. It's really quite sad when you think about it. 

But, um... have I felt this low before? I don't know. Maybe? It's hard to remember. I just know that right now, everything feels like wading through wet cement.
Have you had periods like this before, where you felt low and uninterested in things?

I know you just asked me that, and I am really trying to dig deep and think. It's just... I honestly can't say for sure. I try to look back at my life, you know, my thirties and forties, to see if I felt this way, but I was just so busy then. 

I actually got my bachelor's degree in art history around that time. Which is a bit ironic when you think about it, because I ended up spending my life managing the home goods section of a retail store. But art history was just fascinating. I had this one professor, Dr. Harrison, and he had this enormous, bushy mustache that would twitch whenever he got excited about a painting. It looked exactly like one of those woolly bear caterpillars resting on his upper lip. He used to bring in those old slide projectors for his lectures—do you remember those? With the heavy round carousels? They would click so loudly, and his carousel would always, without fail, get jammed right in the middle of the Italian Renaissance. We'd be sitting there in the pitch dark for ten minutes while he fiddled with the machine, just muttering to himself about modern technology. And that was the nineties! Imagine him trying to use a smartphone today. My granddaughter tried to show me how to use TikTok last week and I just handed the phone right back to her. 

But... oh dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I am so sorry, my mind just keeps drifting away. To answer your question... I really just don't know if I've had a spell like this before. If I did, it didn't stick in my memory. I just can't give you a straight yes or no.
Have you ever felt this low and uninterested in things before this six-month period?

I'm so sorry, doctor. You're being very patient with me. I know you're trying to get a timeline here, and I'm just... I'm really drawing a blank. I honestly don't know if I've ever felt this completely drained and uninterested before this current stretch. 

It's funny how memory works, isn't it? I can remember perfectly the pattern of the wallpaper in my childhood bedroom—little yellow daisies with green stems—but I can't tell you how I felt ten years ago. My mother was the same way. She could recall the exact outfit she wore to a dance in 1955, right down to the pearl buttons on her cardigan, but she'd forget where she put her reading glasses five minutes after setting them down. We used to find them in the strangest places. Once, we found them in the refrigerator, sitting right next to a jar of sweet pickles. She said she was looking for a snack and just got distracted. 

I suppose I get my distractibility from her. She was a wonderful woman, though. Made the best peach cobbler you've ever tasted. The secret was a dash of nutmeg in the crust. Most people just put it in the filling, but she swore by putting it in the crust. 

But, um... no. I really can't say if I've had a period like this before the last six months. I just don't know.
Have you ever experienced a period of feeling low and uninterested in things that lasted for a while and then got better on its own?

I... I really wish I could give you a better answer. I just don't know if I've ever had a time where I felt this awful and then it just... lifted. 

It makes me think of the weather back home in Ohio. You know, you'd get these terrible, gray winters that felt like they were never going to end. Just weeks of slush and that bone-chilling wind off the lake. And then, one day in April, you'd wake up and the sun would be out, and the crocuses would be pushing up through the last bit of snow in the front yard. We had these beautiful purple ones that my husband planted the year we bought the house. He spent an entire Saturday on his hands and knees in the dirt, complaining about his back the whole time. He always said he had a bad back, but he still managed to play golf every Sunday morning. Eighteen holes, walking the course! I always told him, 'Arthur, if you can walk five miles chasing a little white ball, you can certainly help me carry the groceries in.' 

But he was a good man. He just had his priorities, I suppose. 

Anyway... I'm doing it again. I'm sorry. To answer your question... no, I really don't recall a time where I felt this low and then it just got better on its own. I just don't know.
Have you ever felt this low and uninterested in things before this six-month period and then gotten better without treatment?

I know you are really trying to get a clear picture here, and I feel just awful that I keep giving you the same sort of non-answer. Did I ever feel this way before and then get better without a doctor's help? I... I try to think about it, and my mind just completely wanders off. 

Talking about things getting better without treatment, it actually reminds me of my old regional manager at the store, Susan. She was one of those people who thought every problem could just fix itself if you ignored it long enough, or maybe if you just slapped a bright yellow clearance sticker on it. We had this one terrible incident where the sprinkler system malfunctioned right over the premium bedding aisle. It just absolutely soaked thousands of dollars of goose-down comforters. Have you ever smelled wet goose down? It is not pleasant. It smells like a damp basement mixed with a wet dog. 

But Susan, bless her heart, she refused to call the corporate maintenance team to file a proper loss report. She thought if we just pointed some industrial box fans at the shelves overnight, they'd dry out and we could sell them at a discount. She was a very stubborn woman. She always wore these incredibly loud, neon floral blouses, too—the kind that practically gave you a migraine just looking at them during our morning staff meetings. 

Oh dear, there I go again. I am so sorry, I know you don't need to hear about wet blankets and Susan's wardrobe. You have the patience of a saint. To get back to what you were actually asking... I really just can't remember a time before these last six months where I felt this down and then just bounced back on my own. If it happened, I just don't have any memory of it.
Have you experienced more than one period in your life where you felt this low and uninterested in things?

I... I really wish I could give you a different answer this time. I know you're trying to figure out if this has happened multiple times, but my mind is just a complete blank. I honestly don't know if I've had more than one period like this. 

It's so frustrating when your memory just won't cooperate. It reminds me of trying to organize the stockroom at work. We get these huge shipments in right before the holidays, and it's just a mountain of cardboard boxes. You try to keep it organized, you know, electronics over here, seasonal decor over there. But then the seasonal hires come in, and they just start shoving things wherever they fit. You ask them, "Where did you put the extra string lights?" and they just look at you with this blank stare. I had this one girl, Madison—sweet girl, but she spent half her shift texting her boyfriend. I'd ask her a question, and it was like talking to a brick wall. She had these huge, fake eyelashes that looked like caterpillars resting on her eyelids. I don't know how she could even keep her eyes open with the weight of those things. 

But, um... anyway. I'm sorry. I'm doing it again. I just... I don't know if I've felt this low more than once. I really don't.

patient.answer:
Hi. Thank you. Well, what finally scared me into making this appointment is... I've been having these thoughts lately. Like, I'll just be sitting there and I think, "If I didn't wake up tomorrow, that might be easier." I definitely don't want to hurt myself! I really don't. It just... it spooked me to catch myself thinking that way. 

Which is funny because usually nothing spooks me. I'm a supervisor in retail, and let me tell you, you see absolutely everything there. Just last week we had a woman try to return a blender she clearly bought in, like, 2015. She didn't even have a receipt, and she yelled at my newest cashier for twenty minutes. I had to step in, and honestly, I have a bachelor's degree, I really shouldn't be arguing with people about ten-year-old kitchen appliances at my age, but that's retail for you. The general public is just wild sometimes. They really don't read the store policies. 

But anyway, yes... those thoughts about just not waking up. I figured I should probably come in and talk to someone about that.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I suppose so. Most mornings lately, I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling... it's just like the color has completely drained out of everything before I even get dressed for the store.
